results.question: According to the symposium summary in "IAU Symposium 405: Traversing the Galactic Center in Space and Time", what processes explain why the large molecular gas reservoir of the Central Molecular Zone does not produce a luminous Sgr A*, and how do those processes relate to star formation in the CMZ (including the presence of young massive stars in the central parsec)?
results.reference_answer: The symposium summary explains that although the Galactic bar channels large amounts of gas into the inner Galaxy, only a tiny fraction reaches Sgr A*. The majority of inflowing material is instead (1) converted into stars in the CMZ, (2) dispersed by stellar winds and supernova explosions, and (3) expelled via outflows from the hot accretion flow surrounding Sgr A*. These feedback-regulated processes operate across spatial scales and reduce the fuel available for black-hole accretion, producing the extremely low luminosity of Sgr A*. At the same time, the CMZ’s high gas densities, turbulence and strong magnetic fields create conditions similar to high-redshift starbursts, enabling active star formation — which accounts for young massive stars observed within the central parsec despite the region’s strong tidal field (the ‘‘paradox of youth’’). (Citations: 8f89309050d61336c355c0fb, 1411fce74e47b4693334a531)
results.answer: The symposium summary explains that although the Galactic bar channels gas towards the inner Galaxy, only a small fraction reaches the supermassive black hole Sgr A* due to feedback mechanisms. Much of the inflowing material is converted into stars, dispersed by stellar winds and supernova explosions, or expelled through outflows from the hot accretion flow surrounding Sgr A*, which results in Sgr A*'s low luminosity despite the large molecular gas reservoir in the CMZ. This process influences star formation by turning inflowing gas into stars even in extreme conditions, which explains the presence of young massive stars within the central parsec despite the intense tidal forces, illustrating that star formation persists under these energetic conditions.

## **From the Central Molecular Zone to the event horizon** 

One of the central questions discussed at the symposium concerned the striking contrast between the vast molecular gas reservoir of the CMZ and the extremely low luminosity of Sgr A* (talks by Steven Longmore and Mark Morris). Although the Galactic bar efficiently channels gas towards the inner Galaxy, only a tiny fraction ultimately reaches the black hole. Instead, much of the inflowing material is converted into stars, dispersed by stellar winds and supernova explosions, or expelled through outflows from the hot accretion flow surrounding Sgr A* [2]. The Galactic Center therefore appears to regulate itself through feedback operating across many spatial scales (Zixuan Feng). This perspective also reshapes our understanding of star formation. The CMZ provides a nearby laboratory for studying star formation under conditions resembling those in high-redshift starburst galaxies, with unusually high gas densities, turbulence and magnetic fields. Yet fundamental questions remain unresolved. Young massive stars are observed within the central parsec (Zo¨e Haggard) despite the intense tidal field of Sgr A* and the extreme physical conditions of the surrounding circumnuclear medium [the “paradox of youth”; 3]. At IAU Symposium 405 in Brno, the Galactic Center emerged as a nearby laboratory for galactic nuclei, linking the central supermassive black hole, dense stellar populations and multiphase gas into a connected ecosystem across space and time. 

The Galactic Center is often identified with its central supermassive black hole, Sgr A*. Yet the black hole governs gravitationally only the innermost few parsecs of the Milky Way, while the surrounding Nuclear Star Cluster, Nuclear Stellar Disc and Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) shape the dynamics of stars and gas on progressively larger scales. Understanding how these components interact is essential not only for reconstructing the history of our own Galaxy, but also for interpreting galactic nuclei more generally.

results.question: According to "Constraints on the fuzzy dark matter mass using globular clusters in dwarf galaxies from Euclid ERO data", what upper limits on the fuzzy dark matter particle mass parameter m_22 did the authors derive from Euclid ERO globular-cluster candidates for the Fornax and Perseus galaxy clusters and for the Fornax dwarf spheroidal (dSph), and how do the authors summarize the consistency of these constraints with other astrophysical probes?
results.reference_answer: The paper reports three upper limits on m_22 derived from Euclid ERO globular-cluster candidates: m_22 ≤ 1.46^{+0.51}_{-0.00}, m_22 ≤ 1.09^{+0.21}_{-0.00}, and m_22 ≤ 1.38^{+0.48}_{-0.00} for the Fornax and Perseus galaxy clusters and for the Fornax dSph respectively. The authors state these constraints are broadly consistent with constraints inferred from the Milky Way disk and stellar dynamics of nearby dwarf galaxies, but remain in tension with constraints derived from stellar streams and the Lyman-α forest. (evidence: ddf71676ff9029e4c5534bca; c3d05f2f045b4bdbcb084059)
results.answer: The authors derived upper limits on the fuzzy dark matter particle mass parameter m_22 of 1.46 in the Fornax cluster and 1.09 in the Perseus cluster based on Euclid ERO globular-cluster candidates. For the Fornax dwarf spheroidal (dSph), the constraints are compatible with the upper limits of 1 from Marsh & Pop (2015) and 0.4 from González-Morales et al. (2017), but are in tension with the lower bounds from stellar streams (<1.5) and the larger values derived from Lyman-α forest (7-20). The authors note that their constraints are broadly consistent with some studies but in tension with others, reflecting differences in the methods and astrophysical probes used.

## **ABSTRACT** 

We constrain the particle mass of the fuzzy dark matter model using globular cluster candidates in dwarf galaxies, from the Euclid Early Release Observations, within the Fornax and Perseus galaxy clusters. We model the orbital evolution of globular clusters by combining fuzzy dark matter density profiles with the corresponding dynamical friction formalism, and integrate their orbits using `galpy` . In the fuzzy dark matter framework, both the halo density profile and the dynamical friction force are modified by the wave-like nature of the ultra-light dark matter particle, whose mass is parameterized as _m_ 22 = _m_ χ/10[−][22] , eV and explored over the range 0.1 ≤ _m_ 22 ≤ 100. This framework naturally alleviates the long-standing globular cluster timing problem originally identified in the Fornax dSph. We find that globular clusters no longer experience orbital decay toward the centers of their host galaxies for _m_ 22 ≤ 1.46[+] −[0] 0[.] .[51] 32[in the Fornax cluster and] _[ m]_[22][≤][1][.][09][+] −[0] 0[.] .[14] 21[in the Perseus cluster. Future Euclid data releases, providing substantially] larger samples of globular cluster candidates, will enable significantly tighter constraints on the dark matter particle mass within the fuzzy dark matter scenario. 

**Key words.** Dark matter - Galaxy dynamics - Globular clusters - Euclid - Methods: Orbital integrations

retrieved_chunks.text:
The central parsec adds another level of complexity. A companion contribution in this volume by Thorsbro and collaborators discusses high-resolution abundance measurements of stars projected close to Sgr A*. Those data include an old, subsolar-metallicity star with low [α/Fe] as well as metal-rich stars that may remain α-enhanced. Such heterogeneity is naturally difficult to fit into a single closed enrichment sequence. It is instead compatible with a nucleus that combines stars formed in situ from rapidly enriched gas with populations transported inward from the inner bulge, nuclear stellar disc, disrupted clusters, or other early building blocks. Bar-driven inflow can feed the Central Molecular Zone, but transport onward into the central tens of parsecs is model-dependent and may require additional processes beyond the large-scale bar flow (Tress et al. 2020). 

The light elements offer a particularly clean future discriminator. In Liller 1 and Terzan 5, the absence of a Na–O or related light-element anticorrelation argues against a conventional globular-cluster origin (Origlia et al. 2011; Alvarez Garay et al. 2024). The corresponding experiment has not yet been carried out for a sufficiently large, homogeneous NSC sample. Detecting a substantial population with genuine globular-cluster light-element anomalies would directly support an important cluster-infall contribution; their absence would make the old NSC chemically more BFF- or bulge-like.

## **What is next for the Galactic Center** 

The meeting helped identify several major challenges for the coming decade (Mark Morris). These include the origin of the young stars in the central parsec, possible ongoing star formation near Sgr A*, the manifestation of nuclear outflows, the demographics of stellar remnants and intermediatemass black holes, the apparent scarcity of pulsars, and the role of magnetic fields in linking horizonscale accretion to Galactic-scale structures.
